passages.t: No dew or rain, and ravens by a brook
passages.happening:
Elijah the Tishbite, from among the settlers of Gilead, comes to Ahab and swears by the living LORD, the God of Israel before whom he stands: “there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!” (verse 1).

Then the LORD tells him to go east and hide by the Brook of Cherith, east of the Jordan: ‘I have commanded the ravens to feed you there’ (verse 4). Elijah goes. “The ravens would bring him bread and meat in the morning and evening, and he would drink from the brook” (verse 6). After a while the brook dries up, because there has been no rain in the land (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 16 ended with Ahab building a temple for Baal, the god believed to send the rain. Elijah appears without introduction and challenges that belief head on: the LORD, not Baal, rules the dew and the rain. Dew and rain were exactly Baal's domain in the belief of Israel's neighbors, and in a land that lived on winter rain and summer dew, not on rivers, a drought touched everyone.

Elijah's name means that the LORD is his God. His oath, as surely as the LORD lives, is a direct challenge to a religion in which Baal was said to die and rise with the seasons. In a drought, the question of which god truly lives was a matter of survival.

Elijah is from Tishbe in Gilead, east of the Jordan. Where Tishbe lay is not known, and neither is the Brook of Cherith. The setting is Ahab's reign, about 874 to 853 BC.

Ravens were unclean birds under Israel's law, an unlikely set of providers. Before the public contest of chapter 18, the chapter shows the LORD's power in hidden places, and shows the prophet himself living by the word he speaks, fed day by day.
passages.later: The law had warned that turning to other gods would shut the sky: ‘He will shut the heavens so that there will be no rain’ (Deuteronomy 11:17). James holds up Elijah's prayer: ‘He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years’ (James 5:17).
passages.asks: Elijah announced the drought and then had to live through it himself, fed one day at a time. Ask whether you trust God for today's bread or only for a store of it. And ask where, in your own life, you have looked to something other than God for the rain.

passages.t: A widow's last flour and oil
passages.happening:
The word of the LORD comes again: “Get up and go to Zarephath of Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to provide for you” (verse 9). At the town gate Elijah finds a widow gathering sticks and asks her for water and a piece of bread (verses 10-11).

She answers that she has no bread, ‘only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug’ (verse 12). She is gathering sticks to make a last meal for herself and her son before they die. “Do not be afraid,” Elijah says (verse 13). She is to make him a small loaf first and then make some for herself and her son, for the LORD says that the jar of flour will not run out and the jug of oil will not run dry until he sends rain (verses 13-14).

She does as Elijah says, and there is food every day for Elijah, the woman and her household. “The jar of flour was not exhausted and the jug of oil did not run dry, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Elijah” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Zarephath lay on the coast between Tyre and Sidon, in the heartland of the Phoenician kingdom from which Jezebel came. God takes his prophet into Baal's own country, and the drought has reached it too.

A widow in that world was among the most vulnerable people there were, usually without land or income and dependent on relatives or charity. Israel's law commands care for the widow, the orphan and the foreigner again and again. This widow is a foreigner too, and her words describe the last meal before starving. God commands the poorest person in the story to feed his prophet.

Hospitality to a traveler was a sacred duty. She gives first, before she sees the flour last.
passages.later: Jesus used this story in his first sermon at Nazareth: “But I tell you truthfully that there were many widows in Israel in the time of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three and a half years and great famine swept over all the land. Yet Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon” (Luke 4:25-26). His hometown was furious that God's mercy would go to an outsider.
passages.asks: A starving foreign widow fed God's prophet from her last handful of flour. Ask what God might be asking you to give before you can see how you will be provided for. And ask whom you would have passed over as too poor, or too foreign, to be part of God's work.

passages.happening:
Later the widow's son falls ill, and his sickness grows worse until no breath is left in him (verse 17). She cries out to Elijah, the man of God, “what have you done to me? Have you come to remind me of my iniquity and cause the death of my son?” (verse 18).

“Give me your son,” Elijah says (verse 19). He carries the boy to the upper room where he is staying and lays him on his own bed. He cries out to the LORD, “O LORD my God, have You also brought tragedy on this widow who has opened her home to me, by causing her son to die?” (verse 20). He stretches himself over the child three times and cries out again, and ‘the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child’s life returned to him, and he lived’ (verse 22).

Elijah carries him down and gives him to his mother: “Look, your son is alive” (verse 23). She says, “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is truth” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The widow's fear in verse 18 reflects a common belief that a holy man's presence could expose hidden sin and bring it to God's attention. The narrator records her guilt-stricken words without agreeing with them.

Elijah's prayer is honest to the point of accusation. He asks whether God has brought this tragedy on the very woman who took him in. God hears the voice of Elijah.

The chapter is built in three scenes, the brook, the jar and the son, each moving from a word of the LORD to its fulfillment. The word of the LORD comes up again and again, and the chapter ends with the widow's confession that the word of the LORD in Elijah's mouth is truth, in Hebrew emet, something that can bear weight. The scenes deepen as they go: provision in the wilderness, provision in a household, and at last life given back from death.
passages.later: Luke tells of Jesus raising a widow's only son at Nain, and uses the same words: ‘Then Jesus gave him back to his mother’ (Luke 7:15). Hebrews remembers that ‘Women received back their dead, raised to life again’ (Hebrews 11:35), and the stories behind those words include this one.
passages.hard:
Why would God let the son of the widow who sheltered his prophet die?

Elijah himself asks this, and the text does not give a full answer. It does not say that the boy died because of the widow's sin, though she feared it; her guilt-stricken words are recorded, not approved. What the story does show is that the death became the turning point of her faith. She had eaten from the jar for many days, but only after her son was given back did she say that the word of the LORD is truth.

Interpreters caution against reading this as a rule that every loss has a purpose that can be seen. The chapter records a real loss, an honest and anguished prayer, and a God who answered. It leaves room for the reader's own questions, as it left room for Elijah's.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The widow believed her son's death was a punishment, and Elijah took his own question straight to God. Ask what fear or guilt you have let explain a loss for you. And ask whether you dare to pray as honestly as Elijah did.
